- When sentiment is strongly bullish (≥0.67) and model forecast is flat or rising slowly, adjust upward by 1–3% to account for sentiment-driven momentum.
- After a sharp spike in price (e.g., >5% from prior day), model should not overreact — cap forecast slope to avoid overshoot; reduce rate of increase by 10–20%.
- If official event balance is heavily bearish (bearish > bullish by 20+), model should not ignore sentiment decay — reduce forecast mean by 2–5% relative to prior period.
- When sentiment swings from bullish to bearish (e.g., -1.00 to 0.00), model should not lag — adjust forecast downward by 1–3% immediately after sentiment flip.
- For 30-day horizon, if true outcome shows mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 days of decline after peak), model should reduce forecast slope by 10–20% to avoid over-optimism.
- If supply_net is negative and bearish sentiment dominates, model should not assume continuation — add 1–2% downward bias to forecast to reflect supply constraints.
- When multiple recent auctions (e.g., 3+ in 10d) are scheduled, model should not ignore event-driven volatility — add 1–3% volatility buffer to forecast range.
